These cases all present the question whether “major” questions of “vast 
economic and pohtical significance” should be subject to a different statutory 
analysis from ordinary, run-of-the-mill cases—and if so, why.
2. 
Justice Gorsuch's Justification for the Major Questions Doctrine. In a 
separate concurrence in West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 735 (2022), Justice 
Gorsuch (joined by Justice Alito) justified the major questions doctrine as a 
tool “to protect foimdational constitutional guarantees.” Citing Article I’s 
vesting of “legislative powers” in Congress and the Court’s nondelegation 
cases, Gorsuch reasoned that “[m]uch as constitutional rules about retroactive 
legislation and sovereign immunity have their corollary clear-statement rules. 
Article I’s Vesting Clause has its own: the major questions doctrine.”
In his opimon. Justice Gorsuch claimed that “[s]ome version of’ the major 
questions doctrine ‘can be traced to at least 1897, when this Court confronted 
a case involving the Interstate Commerce Commission.” In the case, ICC v. 
Cincinnati, N.O. & T.P.R. Co., 167 U.S. 479, 499 (1897), the Court deemed the 
ICC s claim to set carriage prices for railroads “a power of supreme delicacy 
and importance and reasoned that the fact “[t]hat Congress has transferred 
such a power to any administrative body is not to be presumed or implied from 
any doubtful and uncertain language,” because, “if Congress had intended to 
grant such a power to the [agency], it cannot be doubted that it would have 
used language open to no misconstruction, but clear and direct.” Justice 
Gorsuch also observed that the Court had enforced the nondelegation doctrine 
through “the interpretation of statutory texts, and, more particularly, [by] 
giving narrow constructions to statutory delegations that might otherwise be 
thought to be unconstitutional.” Mistretta v. United States, 488 U.S. 361, 373 
n.7 (1989).
In a nutshell. Justice Gorsuch’s defense of the major questions doctrine 
piggybacked off a claim that Article I incorporates a nondelegation doctrine, 
which (he claimed) could be implemented through statutory interpretation. As 
a result. Justice Gorsuch’s defense of the major questions doctrine depended 
on his approach to the nondelegation doctrine, as expressed in his separate 
dissenting opimon in Gundy v. United States, 588 U.S. 128 (2019), which we 
discussed in Chapter 2. If the major questions doctrine is a mechanism to 
enforce the nondelegation doctrine via statutory interpretation, then it would 
appear to follow that the doctrine’s domain should track the test for the 
nondelegation doctrine’s domain. Consider, in this respect. Justice Gorsuch’s 
articulation of the test for the nondelegation doctrine in Gundy, with its 
emphasis on government coercion of private conduct. How, if at all, does that 
approach to the nondelegation doctrine fit with the application of the major 
questions doctrine in a case involving government benefits, such as Biden v. 
Nebraska?
